G2.angles.01.text: Two angles of a triangle are {a|degree|degrees|degrees} and {b|degree|degrees|degrees}. How big is the third angle, in degrees?
solution: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
The two known angles make {a} + {b} = {=a+b}.

That leaves 180 − {a} = {=180-a} for the two base angles.

G2.angles.10.text: A path goes up like a staircase and has {a|step|steps|steps}. Each step goes up and then to the right. How many right-angle turns are there along the whole path?

G3.symmetry.02.text: The number {a} is marked on a number line. A mirror stands at {b}. Which number is the reflection of {a}?
solution: The distance from {a} to the mirror is {b} − {a} = {=b-a}.
The reflection is behind the mirror at the same distance, so from {b} we go another {=b-a}.
So the reflection of {a} is the number {r}.
hints: The mirror stands between the number and its reflection, so the reflection is on the other side of {b}.
Find the distance from {a} to {b}, then go the same distance on from {b}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.distance-only: {w_distance_only} is the distance from {a} to the mirror. The reflection is the same distance again behind the mirror: {b} + {w_distance_only} = {r}.
explain.mirror-itself: {w_mirror_itself} is the point where the mirror stands, not the reflection of {a}: {b} + {=b-a} = {r}.
explain.wrong-side: {w_wrong_side} comes from going from {a} away from the mirror. The reflection is behind the mirror: {b} + {=b-a} = {r}.

G3.symmetry.03.text: A point stands on the grid at position ({a}; {b}). The vertical grid line number {c} is a line of symmetry. At which position does the mirror point stand? Write the first coordinate, then the second, separated by a semicolon.
solution: The line of symmetry is vertical, so the point is reflected left and right and its height does not change: the second coordinate stays {b}.
From the point to the line it is {c} − {a} = {=c-a|square|squares|squares}, and the same distance on the other side of the line.
The first coordinate of the reflection is {c} + {=c-a} = {=2*c-a}.
So the mirror point stands at position {r}.
hints: The line is vertical, so the height of the point stays the same.
The point is {=c-a|square|squares|squares} from the line. Go the same distance on the other side of the line.
Answer: {r}.

explain.same-point: Position {w_same_point} is the point itself, but we need the mirror point.
explain.swapped: Position {w_swapped} has the two coordinates in the opposite order, but the first coordinate always comes first.
explain.on-the-axis: Position {w_on_the_axis} lies right on the line, but the mirror point is on the other side of the line at the same distance: {=c-a} squares beyond it.
explain.horizontal-mirror: Position {w_horizontal_mirror} comes from reflecting in a horizontal line, but this line is vertical. The height stays {b} and the first coordinate changes: {r}.

G3.symmetry.04.text: Point A stands at position ({a}; {b}) and point O at position ({c}; {d}) is the centre of symmetry. At which position does the point stand that is the reflection of A in O? Write the first coordinate, then the second, separated by a semicolon.
solution: The centre is exactly halfway between a point and its reflection, so we work on each coordinate separately.
First: from {a} to {c} is {c} − {a} = {=c-a}, and the same again: {c} + {=c-a} = {=2*c-a}.
Second: from {b} to {d} is {d} − {b} = {=d-b}, and the same again: {d} + {=d-b} = {=2*d-b}.
So the reflected point stands at position {r}.
hints: Reflect in the centre one coordinate at a time.
O is halfway between A and its reflection. Go from A to O in the first coordinate ({a} to {c}) and in the second ({b} to {d}), then go on the same distance again.
Answer: {r}.

explain.centre: Position {w_centre} is the centre itself, but we need the reflected point.
explain.line-mirror: Position {w_line_mirror} changes only the first coordinate, but reflecting in a centre changes both.
explain.horizontal-mirror: Position {w_horizontal_mirror} changes only the second coordinate, but reflecting in a centre changes both.

G3.symmetry.05.text: Which of these letters have a vertical line of symmetry? 1) A; 2) R; 3) T; 4) B. Answer with the numbers of all the options that fit, separated by commas.
solution: A vertical line of symmetry splits a letter into a left half and a right half that must match like a mirror image.
A and T have identical left and right halves.
R and B have different halves: R has a bump and a leg only on the right, and B has its bulges only on the right.
So the answer is options {r}: A and T.
hints: A vertical line of symmetry splits a letter into a left half and a right half. Imagine folding each letter along that line.
Check A, R, T and B one by one: do the left and right halves match?
Answer: {r}.

explain.only-the-first: {w_only_the_first} is not complete: the left and right halves of T match too.
explain.only-the-third: {w_only_the_third} is not complete: the left and right halves of A match too.
explain.with-the-fourth: {w_with_the_fourth} has one option too many: B has no vertical line of symmetry, because its bulges are only on the right.

G3.symmetry.06.text: Which of these letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? 1) E; 2) L; 3) B; 4) F. Answer with the numbers of all the options that fit, separated by commas.
solution: A horizontal line of symmetry splits a letter into a top half and a bottom half that must match like a mirror image.
E and B have the same top and bottom.
L and F have different tops and bottoms: L has its foot only at the bottom, and F has its top bar and middle bar only in the top half.
So the answer is options {r}: E and B.
hints: A horizontal line of symmetry splits a letter into a top half and a bottom half. Imagine folding each letter along that line.
Check E, L, B and F one by one: do the top and the bottom match?
Answer: {r}.

explain.only-the-first: {w_only_the_first} is not complete: the top and bottom of B match too.
explain.only-the-third: {w_only_the_third} is not complete: the top and bottom of E match too.
explain.with-the-second: {w_with_the_second} has one option too many: the top and bottom of L are different, because the foot is only at the bottom.

G3.symmetry.07.text: Which of these letters has two lines of symmetry? 1) T; 2) E; 3) H; 4) R. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: Two lines of symmetry means a vertical one and a horizontal one together.
T has only a vertical line, E has only a horizontal line, and R has none.
H has both: you can fold it in half from top to bottom and from left to right.
So the answer is option {r}, the letter H.
hints: Two lines of symmetry means the letter can be folded in half in two ways: one vertical, one horizontal.
For each letter ask: does a vertical fold work? Does a horizontal fold work? Which letter passes both tests?
Answer: {r}.

explain.one-vertical-axis: Option {w_one_vertical_axis} is T. It can be folded only along a vertical line, so it has one line of symmetry, not two.
explain.one-horizontal-axis: Option {w_one_horizontal_axis} is E. It can be folded only along a horizontal line, so it has one line of symmetry, not two.
explain.no-axis: Option {w_no_axis} is R. It cannot be folded in half so that the halves match, so it has no line of symmetry.

G3.symmetry.08.text: {c|identical rectangle|identical rectangles|identical rectangles} were cut out, with sides of {a} cm and {b} cm. How many lines of symmetry do all these rectangles have together?
solution: A rectangle can be folded in half in two ways: along and across, through the middles of opposite sides.
It cannot be folded along a diagonal: the sides of {a} cm and {b} cm are different, and the corners would not match.
One rectangle has two lines and there are {c} rectangles: 2 × {c} = {=2*c}.
So there are {r} lines of symmetry altogether.
hints: A rectangle can be folded in half along a line through the middles of opposite sides. A diagonal is not a line of symmetry.
One rectangle has two such lines, and there are {c} rectangles. Put these together.
Answer: {r}.

explain.as-a-square: {w_as_a_square} comes from counting the two diagonals of each rectangle as lines of symmetry too. A diagonal is not a line of symmetry here, because the sides of {a} cm and {b} cm are different.
explain.one: {w_one} comes from noticing only one line for each rectangle. There is another line through the middles of the other two sides: {c} × 2 = {r}.

G3.symmetry.09.text: Some triangles were cut out: {a|isosceles triangle|isosceles triangles|isosceles triangles}, which have only two equal sides, {b|equilateral triangle|equilateral triangles|equilateral triangles}, and {c|scalene triangle|scalene triangles|scalene triangles}, which have sides that are all different. How many lines of symmetry do all these triangles have together?
solution: An isosceles triangle has one line of symmetry: from the vertex between the equal sides to the middle of the third side.
An equilateral triangle has three, one from each vertex. A scalene triangle has none: the halves never match along any line.
So all the triangles have {r|line of symmetry|lines of symmetry|lines of symmetry} together.
hints: How many lines of symmetry does each kind of triangle have?
Multiply the number of lines by the number of triangles of each kind: {a} isosceles, {b} equilateral, {c} scalene. Then add.
Answer: {r}.

explain.scalene-with-an-axis: {w_scalene_with_an_axis} comes from counting one line for each scalene triangle. All its sides are different, so it has no line of symmetry.
explain.equilateral-with-one-axis: {w_equilateral_with_one_axis} comes from counting only one line for each equilateral triangle. It has three, one through each vertex.
explain.one-axis-each: {w_one_axis_each} gives one line to every triangle. But an equilateral triangle has three and a scalene one has none.

G3.symmetry.10.text: A sheet of paper is folded in half {a|time|times|times}, each time along a new fold line. Then one hole is punched straight through it, not on a fold, and the sheet is unfolded. How many holes are there?
solution: Each fold doubles the number of layers: we multiply by 2 once for every fold.
There are {a} folds. Before the last fold there were {=pow(2,a-1)|layer|layers|layers}, and after it {=pow(2,a-1)} × 2 = {r}.
The hole goes through every layer, so each layer gets a hole.
So the unfolded sheet has {r|hole|holes|holes}.
hints: Each fold stacks the sheet into more layers. How many layers are there after all the folds?
After every fold there are twice as many layers: start with one layer and double it {a|time|times|times}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.one-hole: {w_one_hole} is just one hole, but the punch went through all the layers.
explain.per-fold: {w_per_fold} is the number of folds, but the layers double after every fold.
explain.one-fold-less: {w_one_fold_less} is the number of layers before the last fold. The last fold doubles them once more: {=pow(2,a-1)} × 2 = {r}.

G3.symmetry.11.text: A card with a picture is flipped over {a|time|times|times} in a row, each time along the same line. How does it lie now? 1) as in a mirror; 2) the same as at the start; 3) upside down; 4) turned a quarter turn. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: One flip along a line gives a mirror image of the card, and a second flip along the same line puts it back where it was.
There are {a} flips: pairs of flips {=floor(a/2)}, left-over flips {=mod(a,2)}.
Pairs do not change the card. With no left-over flip it lies as at the start, and with one it lies as in a mirror: option {r} fits.
hints: What does one flip along the line do? And two in a row?
There are {a} flips. Put them in pairs: how many pairs are there, and is one flip left over?
Answer: {r}.

explain.upside-down: Option {w_upside_down} does not fit: a card lies upside down after flips along two different lines, but here the line is always the same.
explain.quarter-turn: Option {w_quarter_turn} does not fit: flipping along a line never turns the card a quarter turn.
explain.the-other-parity: Option {w_the_other_parity} goes with the other number of left-over flips: there are {a} flips, {=floor(a/2)} pairs and {=mod(a,2)} left over.

G3.symmetry.12.text: {a|square|squares|squares} and {b|rectangle|rectangles|rectangles} with sides of different lengths were cut out. How many lines of symmetry do all these shapes have together?
solution: A square has four lines of symmetry: two through the middles of the sides and two diagonals.
A rectangle with different sides has only two lines; the diagonals do not work.
So all the shapes have {r|line of symmetry|lines of symmetry|lines of symmetry} together.

explain.diagonals-of-rectangles: {w_diagonals_of_rectangles} comes from counting the diagonals of the rectangles too. The diagonal of a rectangle with different sides is not a line of symmetry.

Moving up changes the second coordinate: {b} + {d} = {=b+d}.

Add {c} to the first coordinate, {a}, and add {d} to the second coordinate, {b}.

The first coordinate of the middle is halfway between {a} and {b}: ({a} + {b}) : 2 = {=(a+b)/2}.

The first coordinate of the middle is the average of {a} and {b}: add them and divide by 2.

G4.coordinates.06.text: Two opposite vertices of a rectangle with sides along the grid lines stand at positions ({a}; {b}) and ({c}; {d}). What is its area, in squares?

Horizontally {c} − {a} = {=c-a}, vertically {d} − {b} = {=d-b}.

G4.coordinates.07.text: A walker goes along the grid lines, only to the right and up, from position ({a}; {b}) to position ({c}; {d}). How many squares does the walker go along the shortest path?

solution: Each of the two coordinates can be any whole number from 0 to {a}, and zero counts too.

Every value of {x} goes with every value of {y}, so we multiply: {=a+1} × {=a+1} = {=(a+1)*(a+1)}.

G7.plan-1S.08.text: One cell of the plan stands for {a|square metre|square metres|square metres}. A shape on the plan covers {b|cell|cells|cells}. What is its area on the ground, in square metres?

G7.plan-1S.09.text: The side of a grid cell on the map is 1 km. A house is at position ({a}; {b}), a shop at position ({c}; {d}). How many kilometres is it along the grid lines from the house to the shop?

Vertically you go from {b} to {d}: {d} − {b} = {=d-b}.

The horizontal part goes from {a} to {c}, the vertical part from {b} to {d}. How many cells is each?

G7.plan-1S.10.text: A segment {x} km long on the ground is shown on a map as a segment of {b} cm. How many kilometres on the ground does one centimetre of the map stand for?

G1.shapes.13.text: A square is turned and stood on one of its corners. What is the shape now? 1) still the same square; 2) no longer a square, but a different shape; 3) a triangle. Answer with the number of the option.

G2.angles.14.text: Angle A is {a|degree|degrees|degrees}, and its arms are drawn short. Angle B is {b|degree|degrees|degrees}, and its arms are drawn {c|time|times|times} as long. Put a sign between angle A and angle B.

G1.shapes.14.text: In a triangle, {a|segment|segments|segments} are drawn from one vertex to the opposite side. How many triangles are there in the picture, counting the big one?
solution: Together with the two ends of the side the segments go to, there are {=a+2|point|points|points} marked on it.
Every triangle is made of the top vertex and two of these points, so we count pairs of points.
The first point can be chosen in {=a+2} ways and the second in {=a+1} ways, but each pair has been counted twice: {=a+2} × {=a+1} : 2 = {r}.
So there are {r|triangle|triangles|triangles} in the picture.

G1.shapes.15.text: A chequered board is {a} × {b} cells. How many rectangles can you outline along the grid lines? Squares and the whole board count too.
solution: A rectangle is fixed by two vertical grid lines and two horizontal ones.
There are {=b+1} vertical lines, and a pair of them can be chosen in {=b+1} × {b} : 2 = {=(b+1)*b/2} ways.
There are {=a+1} horizontal lines, and a pair of them can be chosen in {=a+1} × {a} : 2 = {=(a+1)*a/2} ways.
Any pair of vertical lines goes with any pair of horizontal lines: {=(b+1)*b/2} × {=(a+1)*a/2} = {r}.

explain.cells-only: {w_cells_only} is only the number of single cells. There are more rectangles, made of two, three or more cells.

G1.shapes.16.text: A convex polygon has {a|vertex|vertices|vertices}. How many diagonals does it have altogether? A diagonal joins two vertices that are not next to each other.
solution: From each vertex, diagonals go to all the vertices except itself and its two neighbours: {a} − 3 = {=a-3}.
From all {a} vertices there are {a} × {=a-3} = {=a*(a-3)} diagonals, but every diagonal has two ends, so it has been counted twice.
Halve it: {=a*(a-3)} : 2 = {r}.
So the polygon has {r|diagonal|diagonals|diagonals}.
hints: How many diagonals leave one vertex? Do not count the vertex itself or its two neighbours.
From one vertex there are {a} − 3 diagonals. Multiply by the {a} vertices, but remember that each diagonal has two ends.
Answer: {r}.

explain.from-one-vertex: {w_from_one_vertex} is the number of diagonals from one vertex only, but the polygon has {a} vertices.

explain.all-segments: {w_all_segments} counts all the segments between vertices, and the sides are among them. Diagonals are only the segments that are not sides.

G1.shapes.17.text: A square with sides of {a} cm is cut by one straight cut, parallel to a side, into two rectangles. What is the sum of the perimeters of these two rectangles, in centimetres?
solution: The perimeter of the whole square is 4 × {a} = {=4*a} cm.
The cut, {a} cm long, becomes a side of both rectangles, so it counts twice in the sum of the perimeters.
That adds 2 × {a} = {=2*a} cm to the perimeter of the square: {=4*a} + {=2*a} = {r}.
So the sum of the perimeters is {r} cm.

The cut, {a} cm long, is a side of one rectangle and also a side of the other. What does that add to the perimeter of the square?

G1.shapes.18.text: The picture shows {a|square|squares|squares}, {b|rectangle|rectangles|rectangles}, {c|triangle|triangles|triangles} and {d|circle|circles|circles}. How many of these shapes have corners?

explain.circles-only: {w_circles_only} is the number of circles. The question asks about the shapes with corners: {a} + {b} + {c} = {r}.

G1.shapes.19.text: What is a polygon with {a} sides called? 1) triangle; 2) quadrilateral; 3) pentagon; 4) hexagon; 5) heptagon; 6) octagon. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: The name of a polygon tells how many sides it has: a triangle has three, a quadrilateral four, a pentagon five, a hexagon six, a heptagon seven and an octagon eight.

G2.angles.15.text: An angle is {a|degree|degrees|degrees}. What kind of angle is it? 1) acute; 2) right; 3) obtuse; 4) straight. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle, and an obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle. A right angle is 90 degrees and a straight angle is 180 degrees.
Compare {a} with 90 and with 180: option {r} fits.

G2.angles.16.text: One arm of an angle lies on the zero mark of the protractor scale, and the other is shown in the picture. How big is the angle, in degrees?
solution: The labelled marks are 30 degrees apart, and between them there are three divisions: each division is 10 degrees.
The arm has passed the labelled mark {=floor(a/30)*30} and then {=(a-floor(a/30)*30)/10|division|divisions|divisions} more.
The angle is {=floor(a/30)*30} + {=(a-floor(a/30)*30)/10} × 10 = {r}.
So the angle is {r|degree|degrees|degrees}.

Find the last labelled mark the arm has passed (the labels are 30 apart) and count the divisions after it, 10 degrees each.

G2.angles.17.text: The clock shows half past {a}. How big is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand, in degrees?
solution: The clock face has 12 hours and 360 degrees, so one hour is 360 : 12 = 30 degrees.
At half past, the minute hand points to 6, which is 6 × 30 = 180 degrees from the top.
The hour hand has gone {a|hour|hours|hours} from the top and another half hour, which is 15 degrees: {a} × 30 + 15 = {=30*a+15}.
Between the hands there are {=max(180,30*a+15)} − {=min(180,30*a+15)} = {r|degree|degrees|degrees}.

The hour hand is {a} × 30 + 15 = {=30*a+15} degrees from the top, and the minute hand is 180 degrees from the top. Find the gap between them.
Answer: {r}.

G2.angles.18.text: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio {u}:{v}:{t}. How big is the biggest angle, in degrees?
solution: Altogether there are {u} + {v} + {t} = {=u+v+t} parts.
The angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, so one part is 180 : {=u+v+t} = {=180/(u+v+t)}.
The biggest angle is {m|part|parts|parts}: {m} × {=180/(u+v+t)} = {r}.
So the biggest angle is {r|degree|degrees|degrees}.

There are {=u+v+t} parts to share 180 degrees. Find one part, then take as many parts as the biggest angle has.
Answer: {r}.

explain.one-part: {w_one_part} is one part, but the biggest angle takes {m|part|parts|parts}: {m} × {w_one_part} = {r}.

G2.angles.19.text: Two straight lines cross and make four angles. Two vertically opposite angles together make {a|degree|degrees|degrees}. How big is each of the other two angles, in degrees?
solution: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so each of them is {a} : 2 = {=a/2}.
The angle next to it makes a straight angle with it, 180 degrees.
The other angle is 180 − {=a/2} = {r}.
So each of the other two angles is {r|degree|degrees|degrees}.
hints: Vertically opposite angles are equal. How many degrees is one of them?
One of them is {a} : 2. The angle next to it makes 180 degrees together with it.
Answer: {r}.

explain.the-vertical-angle: {w_the_vertical_angle} is {a} : 2, one of the first two angles, but the question is about the other two: 180 − {w_the_vertical_angle} = {r}.
explain.from-180-the-sum: {w_from_180_the_sum} comes from taking the sum {a} away from 180, but only one of the two equal angles has to be taken away: 180 − {=a/2} = {r}.

G2.angles.20.text: A straight angle is split by a ray into two angles. One of them is {a|degree|degrees|degrees} bigger than the other. How big is the bigger angle, in degrees?
solution: If we take the extra {a} degrees off the bigger angle, the angles are equal, and together they make 180 − {a} = {=180-a}.
The smaller angle is {=180-a} : 2 = {=(180-a)/2}.
The bigger angle is {=(180-a)/2} + {a} = {r}.
So the bigger angle is {r|degree|degrees|degrees}.
hints: A straight angle is 180 degrees. It is made of two angles, and one is {a} bigger than the other.
Take the difference, {a}, away from the bigger angle: two equal angles are left, together 180 − {a}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.the-smaller-angle: {w_the_smaller_angle} is the smaller angle, but the question asks for the bigger one.
explain.half-plus-difference: {w_half_plus_difference} comes from adding {a} to half of 180. First take the difference away, then halve, and only then add it back: {=(180-a)/2} + {a} = {r}.
explain.just-the-rest: {w_just_the_rest} comes from taking the difference away from 180, but that is two equal angles together. Each of them is half of it, and the difference goes back to the bigger one: {=(180-a)/2} + {a} = {r}.

G2.angles.21.text: A hand turns {a|degree|degrees|degrees} clockwise, then {b|degree|degrees|degrees} anticlockwise, and then another {c|degree|degrees|degrees} clockwise. How many degrees is it turned from where it started?
solution: Turns clockwise move the hand forward and a turn anticlockwise moves it back, so we add the first kind and take away the second.
Total: {a} − {b} + {c} = {=a-b+c}.
So the hand is turned {r|degree|degrees|degrees} from where it started.

First {a} forward, then {b} back, then {c} forward again. Work through them in order.
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-added: {w_all_added} comes from adding all the turns, but the turn anticlockwise takes some away: {a} − {b} + {c} = {r}.
explain.wrong-sign: {w_wrong_sign} comes from adding the anticlockwise turn and taking away the last clockwise one. The signs are swapped: {a} − {b} + {c} = {r}.
explain.all-subtracted: {w_all_subtracted} comes from taking away the last turn as well. It is clockwise like the first turn, so it is added: {a} − {b} + {c} = {r}.

G3.symmetry.13.text: A clock seen in a mirror shows {t}. What time is it really?
solution: A mirror swaps the sides, so the time in the mirror and the real time together make exactly 12:00. The real time is 12:00 − {t}.
Hours: 11 − {a} = {=11-a}, because one hour was used up for the minutes.
So the real time is {r}.
hints: The time in the mirror and the real time together make 12 hours.
Take the mirror time away from 12:00: first the minutes (60 − {b}), then the hours (11 − {a}, because one hour went into the minutes).
Answer: {r}.

explain.the-shown-time: {w_the_shown_time} is the time in the mirror itself, but the real time together with it makes 12:00.
explain.same-minutes: {w_same_minutes}: the hours are found, but the minutes were left as they were. The real minutes are 60 − {b} = {=60-b}.
explain.forgot-the-hour: {w_forgot_the_hour}: the minutes are found, but the hours were taken from 12 without the hour that went into the minutes. The hours are 11 − {a} = {=11-a}.

G3.symmetry.14.text: A rectangle with sides of {a} cm and {b} cm is reflected in a line on which its side of {b} cm lies. The rectangle and its reflection together make one shape. What is the perimeter of this shape, in centimetres?
solution: The rectangle and its reflection touch along the side of {b} cm and together make one big rectangle.
One side of it is {b} cm and the other is twice the side of {a} cm: 2 × {a} = {=2*a}.
Perimeter: 2 × ({=2*a} + {b}) = {r}.
So the perimeter of the shape is {r} cm.
hints: What shape do you get if you put the rectangle next to its reflection?
You get one big rectangle with sides of {b} cm and twice {a} cm. The shared side is inside the shape, so it is not part of the perimeter.
Answer: {r}.

explain.both-perimeters: {w_both_perimeters} is the sum of the perimeters of the two rectangles. The shared side of {b} cm is inside the shape, so it does not count in the perimeter.
explain.one-perimeter: {w_one_perimeter} is the perimeter of one rectangle, but the shape is twice as wide: with its reflection, its side is {=2*a} cm.
explain.area: {w_area} is the area of the shape, but the question asks for the perimeter, the sum of all the sides: 2 × ({=2*a} + {b}) = {r}.

G3.symmetry.15.text: A strip is made of {a|cell|cells|cells}. Each cell is painted blue or white. How many colourings have a vertical line of symmetry, that is, the left half is the mirror image of the right half?
solution: The line of symmetry cuts the strip in half and the colours of the right half repeat the left half in reverse order, so the right half does not have to be chosen. With an odd number of cells the middle cell is on the line and is chosen freely.
Free cells: {=floor((a+1)/2)}, each with two colours.
Every free cell doubles the number of colourings: before the last one there were {=pow(2,floor((a+1)/2)-1)}, and with it {=pow(2,floor((a+1)/2)-1)} × 2 = {r}.
So there are {r} symmetric colourings.
hints: The right half of the strip repeats the left half.
{=floor((a+1)/2)|cell|cells|cells} can be coloured freely, and each has two colours. Every free cell doubles the number of colourings.
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-colourings: {w_all_colourings} is all the colourings together, but we need only the symmetric ones: the right half of the strip repeats the left half.
explain.middle-cell-forgotten: {w_middle_cell_forgotten} is found without the middle cell. It stands on the line and its colour is chosen as well: there are {=floor((a+1)/2)} free cells.
explain.free-cells: {w_free_cells} is the number of free cells, but there are more colourings: each free cell gives two colours.

G3.symmetry.16.text: A number with {a} digits reads the same from left to right and from right to left, like 121 or 1331. How many such numbers are there? The first digit cannot be zero.
solution: The right half of the number repeats the left half in reverse order, so we choose freely only the first {=floor((a+1)/2)|digit|digits|digits}.
The first digit can be anything except zero: 9 ways. Each of the other free digits has ten choices, and there are {=floor((a+1)/2)-1} of them.
In total: 9 × {=pow(10,floor((a+1)/2)-1)} = {r}.
hints: How many digits can you choose freely?
The first digit is not zero and the other free digits can be anything. The first {=floor((a+1)/2)|digit|digits|digits} decide the whole number.
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-numbers: {w_all_numbers} is all the numbers with {a} digits, but we need only those that read the same both ways.
explain.zero-first: {w_zero_first} allows zero as the first digit too. The first digit can be anything except zero: 9 ways.

G3.symmetry.17.text: Point A stands at position ({a}; {b}) and point B at position ({c}; {d}). They are symmetric about the point O. At which position does point O stand? Write the first coordinate, then the second, separated by a semicolon.
solution: The centre of symmetry is exactly halfway between a point and its reflection, so O is the middle of the segment AB.
First coordinate: ({a} + {c}) : 2 = {=(a+c)/2}.
Second coordinate: ({b} + {d}) : 2 = {=(b+d)/2}.
So point O stands at position {r}.
hints: The centre of symmetry is the middle of the segment between a point and its reflection.
Find the middle of each coordinate separately: {a} and {c}, then {b} and {d}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.sum-not-halved: Position {w_sum_not_halved} is made of sums, but the middle lies halfway: each sum has to be halved.

G3.symmetry.18.text: A point stands on the grid at position ({a}; {b}). The horizontal grid line number {c} is a line of symmetry. At which position does the mirror point stand? Write the first coordinate, then the second, separated by a semicolon.
solution: The line is horizontal, so the point is reflected up and down and its place from left to right does not change: the first coordinate stays {a}.
From the point to the line it is {c} − {b} = {=c-b|square|squares|squares}, and the same distance on the other side of the line.
The second coordinate of the reflection is {c} + {=c-b} = {=2*c-b}.
So the mirror point stands at position {r}.

The point is {=c-b|square|squares|squares} below the line. Go the same distance above it.
Answer: {r}.

G4.coordinates.12.text: A point P is marked on a grid. What are its coordinates? Write the first coordinate, then the second, separated by a semicolon.
solution: The first coordinate is the number of squares to the right of the origin, and the second is the number of squares up.

We write the number to the right first, then the number up. So the coordinates of the point are {r}.

Count the squares to the right first, then up. Do not start counting at one.

G4.coordinates.13.text: The vertices of a rectangle with sides along the grid lines stand at positions ({a}; {b}) and ({c}; {d}); these are two opposite vertices. How many grid points lie strictly inside the rectangle, not on its sides?
solution: Only the points that are not on the sides lie inside: in each direction we step in by one from the edges.
Horizontally there are {=c-a|step|steps|steps} between the sides, and the points strictly inside a row are one fewer: {=c-a} − 1 = {=c-a-1|point|points|points}.
Vertically there are {=d-b|step|steps|steps} between the sides, and the points strictly inside a column are one fewer: {=d-b} − 1 = {=d-b-1|point|points|points}.
Inside points altogether: {=c-a-1} × {=d-b-1} = {r}.
hints: Points on the sides must not be counted.
Strictly inside a row there are {=c-a} − 1 points, and there are {=d-b} − 1 such rows. Multiply.
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-points: {w_all_points} counts all the grid points, including those on the sides. Inside there are only {=c-a-1} × {=d-b-1} = {r}.
explain.area: {w_area} is the area of the rectangle in squares, but we need the grid points inside: there are fewer, because we count the points, not the squares between them.
explain.one-direction-only: {w_one_direction_only} takes one away in only one direction. One has to be taken away both horizontally and vertically: {=c-a-1} × {=d-b-1} = {r}.

G4.coordinates.14.text: A counter stands at the origin of the grid, position (0; 0), and goes to position ({u}; {v}). In one move it goes one square to the right or one square up. How many different shortest paths can it take?
solution: You can reach any point of the grid only from the left or from below, so the number of paths to a point is the sum of the numbers of paths to the point on its left and the point below it.
Points on the left and bottom lines have one path each, and then we add the numbers square by square until we reach the goal.
The point to the left of the goal can be reached in {p1|path|paths|paths}, and the point below it in {p2|path|paths|paths}.
To the goal: {p1} + {p2} = {r}.
hints: Every point of the grid is reached from the left or from below. How are the numbers of paths to neighbouring points connected?
Write the number of paths at every point of the grid, starting at the origin: points on the bottom and left lines have one path, then add the numbers from the left and from below.
Answer: {r}.

explain.steps-count: {w_steps_count} is the number of steps in a path, not the number of different paths: the order of the steps right and up can be changed.
explain.two-corner-routes: {w_two_corner_routes} counts only the two paths along the edges, first right and then up, and the other way round. Many more paths go through the middle of the grid.
explain.points-count: {w_points_count} is the number of grid points, not paths: every point has a different number of paths.

G4.coordinates.15.text: A counter stands at the origin of the grid, position (0; 0). In one move it goes to a neighbouring square: right, left, up or down. The counter made exactly {n} moves and never stayed still. At which of these positions could it be? 1) ({x1}; {y1}); 2) ({x2}; {y2}); 3) ({x3}; {y3}); 4) ({x4}; {y4}). Answer with the number of the option.
solution: Each move changes one coordinate by one, so after every move the sum of the coordinates changes between odd and even.

After {n} moves the sum of the distances along the axes is odd or even in the same way as {n}, and it is not more than {n}, because in one move the counter gets at most one square further from the origin.
The sums of the distances for the options are {s1}, {s2}, {s3}, {s4}.
Option {r} fits: its sum is not more than {n} and is odd or even in the same way as {n}.
hints: Does the sum of the coordinates become odd or even in one move? What happens in the next move?
For each option work out the sum of the distances along the axes. Is it not more than {n}, and is it odd or even in the same way as {n}?
Answer: {r}.

explain.wrong-parity: Option {w_wrong_parity} does not fit: the sum of the distances along its axes is odd or even in a different way from the number of moves, {n}.
explain.too-far: Option {w_too_far} does not fit: this position is more than {n} moves from the origin.

G4.coordinates.16.text: The vertices of a triangle stand at positions ({a}; {b}), ({c}; {b}) and ({c}; {d}). What is the area of this triangle, in squares?
solution: The first and second vertices are in the same row, and the second and third are in the same column, so the angle at the second vertex is a right angle and the legs run along the grid lines.
The legs: {c} − {a} = {=c-a} and {d} − {b} = {=d-b}.
The area of a right-angled triangle is half the product of its legs: {=c-a} × {=d-b} : 2 = {r}.
So the area of the triangle is {r|square|squares|squares}.
hints: Find the lengths of the sides that run along the grid lines: {c} − {a} and {d} − {b}.
The triangle is half of the rectangle with the same legs: multiply the legs, then halve.
Answer: {r}.

explain.rectangle-area: {w_rectangle_area} is the area of the rectangle with these legs, and the triangle is half of it.
explain.legs-added: {w_legs_added} is the sum of the legs, but the area is found by multiplying, and then taking half.

G4.coordinates.17.text: How many points with whole-number, positive coordinates ({x}; {y}) lie on the line where the sum of the coordinates {x} + {y} is {a}?
solution: Positive whole coordinates start at one, and the second coordinate is {a} minus the first.
The first coordinate can be any number from 1 to {=a-1}: with a bigger one the second would become zero.
There are exactly {=a-1} numbers from 1 to {=a-1}, one fewer than {a}: {a} − 1 = {r}.
So there are {r} such points.
hints: What can the first and the second coordinate be if their sum is {a}?
The coordinates cannot be zero. For which values of the first coordinate does the second stay positive?
Answer: {r}.

explain.fence-post: {w_fence_post} comes from throwing out too many: every value of the first coordinate from 1 to {=a-1} is allowed, and there are {r}.

G5.solids-nets.14.text: The picture shows four nets made of six squares. Which of them folds into a cube with no gaps and no overlaps? 1) the first; 2) the second; 3) the third; 4) the fourth. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: A net folds into a cube if its six squares become six different faces, so no two squares may land on the same place.
Take one square as the bottom and fold the neighbours up. If a square lands where another one already is, the net does not work.
Checking all four nets this way, only net number {r} folds without overlaps.
hints: A net of a cube is six squares that can be folded into a cube. Fold each net in your head and look for two squares that would land on the same place.
Take one square as the bottom and fold four squares up around it. Where do the last two squares go: one on the lid and one on the empty wall, or both on the same place?
Answer: {r}.

explain.the-first-wrong-net: Net number {w_the_first_wrong_net} does not fold into a cube: two of its squares land on the same face, and another face stays empty.
explain.the-second-wrong-net: Net number {w_the_second_wrong_net} does not fold into a cube: two of its squares land on the same face, and another face stays empty.
explain.the-third-wrong-net: Net number {w_the_third_wrong_net} does not fold into a cube: two of its squares land on the same face, and another face stays empty.

G5.solids-nets.15.text: On the squares of a net of a cube there are dots: each square has its own number from 1 to 6, all different. How many dots will be on the face opposite the face with {k|dot|dots|dots}, once the net is folded into a cube? Choose the number of dots.
solution: Opposite faces of a cube do not touch each other, not even at a corner: four other faces lie between them.
Put the face with {k|dot|dots|dots} on the table as the bottom and fold up the net: the face that becomes the lid is the opposite one.
The lid is the face with {r|dot|dots|dots}.
hints: Opposite faces of a cube never touch; four other faces lie between them. Find the square with {k|dot|dots|dots} on the net.
Take the square with {k|dot|dots|dots} as the bottom and fold the neighbours up. Which square becomes the lid?
Answer: {r}.

explain.a-neighbour-face: {w_a_neighbour_face} is a square that stands next to the right one on the net. After folding it still touches that face, so it is a neighbour, not the opposite face.
explain.seven-minus: {w_seven_minus} comes from the rule of a real die, where opposite faces add up to 7. Here the dots are placed differently, so you find the opposite face by folding the net.

G5.solids-nets.16.text: A cube {a} × {a} × {a} made of equal small cubes is painted on the outside. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
solution: Exactly two faces are painted on the small cubes that sit on the edges of the big cube, but not in a corner: a corner cube has three painted faces.
One edge has {a|cube|cubes|cubes}, and the two at the ends are corner cubes, so {a} − 2 = {=a-2} are left.
A cube has 12 edges: 12 × {=a-2} = {r}.
So {r|cube has|cubes have|cubes have} exactly two painted faces.
hints: You need the small cubes on the edges of the big cube, but not in the corners: a corner cube has three painted faces. Start with one edge.
One edge has {a|cube|cubes|cubes}, and the two at the ends are in corners. How many cubes are between the corners, and how many edges does a cube have?
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-edge-cubes: {w_all_edge_cubes} is 12 × {a}: the corner cubes were counted too, and they have three painted faces. Between the corners of one edge there are {=a-2} of them: 12 × {=a-2} = {r}.
explain.one-edge: {w_one_edge} is the number of cubes on one edge between the corners, but a cube has 12 edges: 12 × {w_one_edge} = {r}.
explain.one-face-answer: {w_one_face_answer} counts the cubes in the middle of the faces, which have one painted face. We need the ones on the edges: 12 × {=a-2} = {r}.

G5.solids-nets.17.text: A cube {a} × {a} × {a} made of equal small cubes is painted on the outside. How many small cubes are not painted at all?
solution: The unpainted cubes are the ones inside: none of their faces is on the outside.
Take one layer off each of the six sides of the big cube and a cube with side {a} − 2 = {=a-2} is left.
So {r|cube is|cubes are|cubes are} not painted at all.
hints: Look for the cubes with none of their faces on the outside; they are hidden inside the big cube.
Take a layer off each of the six sides. In one row, how many cubes are left when you remove one from each end?
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-cubes: {w_all_cubes} is all the cubes of the big cube, but the ones on the outside are painted.
explain.one-layer: {w_one_layer} is the number of cubes in one layer inside, but the inner cube is {=a-2} such layers thick: {=a-2} × {=a-2} × {=a-2} = {r}.
explain.layer-off: {w_layer_off} is a cube with side {=a-1}: a layer was taken off only one side in each direction. The layer comes off both sides, so the inner cube has side {a} − 2 = {=a-2}, and the number of cubes in it is {r}.

G5.solids-nets.18.text: Every edge of a polyhedron lies on exactly two of its faces. The polyhedron has {t|triangular face|triangular faces|triangular faces}, {s|quadrilateral face|quadrilateral faces|quadrilateral faces} and {f|pentagonal face|pentagonal faces|pentagonal faces}, and no other faces. How many edges does it have?
solution: Count the sides of all the faces: triangles {t} × 3 = {=3*t}, quadrilaterals {s} × 4 = {=4*s}, pentagons {f} × 5 = {=5*f}.
In all there are {=3*t} + {=4*s} + {=5*f} = {=3*t+4*s+5*f} sides.
Every edge was counted twice, once in each of its two faces, so there are half as many edges: {=3*t+4*s+5*f} : 2 = {r}.
So the polyhedron has {r|edge|edges|edges}.
hints: Every edge is a side shared by two faces. How many sides do all the faces have together, counted one face at a time?
The faces have triangles {t} × 3, quadrilaterals {s} × 4 and pentagons {f} × 5 sides. Add them up, and remember that you counted every edge twice.
Answer: {r}.

explain.sides-counted-once: {w_sides_counted_once} is the number of sides of all the faces together. Every edge is in it twice, once for each of its two faces, so there are half as many edges: {w_sides_counted_once} : 2 = {r}.
explain.faces-count: {w_faces_count} is the number of faces, but the question is about edges. Count the sides of all the faces and halve it: {=3*t+4*s+5*f} : 2 = {r}.

G5.solids-nets.19.text: A cube is sawn into pieces by flat cuts: {a|cut|cuts|cuts} parallel to the top face, {b|cut|cuts|cuts} parallel to the front face and {c|cut|cuts|cuts} parallel to the side face. Into how many pieces does the cube fall apart?
solution: Cuts in one direction divide the cube into layers, and there is one more layer than there are cuts: {a} + 1 = {=a+1}.
In the two other directions there are {=b+1} and {=c+1} layers.
Cuts in the three directions do not get in each other's way, so the numbers of layers are multiplied: {=a+1} × {=b+1} × {=c+1} = {r}.
So the cube falls into {r|piece|pieces|pieces}.
hints: How many layers do the cuts in one direction make? Think: one cut divides a cube into two layers.
Find the number of layers in each direction: {a} + 1, {b} + 1 and {c} + 1. Layers of different directions cross each other.
Answer: {r}.

explain.sum-plus-one: {w_sum_plus_one} is {a} + {b} + {c} + 1, as if all the cuts went one after another in one direction. But cuts in three directions cross, and the numbers of layers multiply.
explain.product-of-cuts: {w_product_of_cuts} is the product of the numbers of cuts, but there is one more layer than there are cuts: {=a+1} × {=b+1} × {=c+1} = {r}.
explain.layers-added: {w_layers_added} is the sum of the numbers of layers {=a+1} + {=b+1} + {=c+1}. Layers of different directions do not add up, they cross, so the numbers of layers are multiplied: {r}.

G6.views.11.text: Three stacks of cubes stand in a row; from left to right they are {a}, {b} and {c|cube|cubes|cubes} high. You walk round the row and look at it from the opposite side. Which stack is on your left now? 1) the stack of height {o1}; 2) the stack of height {o2}; 3) the stack of height {o3}. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: When you walk round the row and look from the other side, the order of the stacks is reversed: the old right stack is now on the left.
From left to right it was {a}, {b}, {c}, and now it is {c}, {b}, {a}.
On the left there is now the stack of height {c}: that is option {r}.
hints: You have walked round the row and now stand on the other side. What is on your left now?
From left to right the stacks were {a}, {b}, {c}. Which one was on the right? From the other side it is on the left.
Answer: {r}.

explain.the-old-left: Option {w_the_old_left} is the stack that was on the left before. From the other side it is on the right.
explain.the-middle: Option {w_the_middle} is the middle stack: it stays in the middle from the other side too.

G6.views.12.text: A plan of a building made of cubes shows the heights of the stacks: in the first row {a} and {b}, in the second row {c} and {d}. The first row is the one nearest to you, the second row is further away. How many squares can you see when you look at the building from the front? Stacks standing one behind the other hide each other.
solution: From the front, the two stacks in one column of the plan stand one behind the other, and you see as many squares as the taller one has.
In the first column, of {a} and {c} the taller is {=max(a,c)}. In the second column, of {b} and {d} the taller is {=max(b,d)}.
Add them: {=max(a,c)} + {=max(b,d)} = {r}.
So you see {r|square|squares|squares} from the front.
hints: From the front the stacks in one column of the plan stand one behind the other. What can you see of each such pair?
In the first column of the plan stand {a} and {c}, in the second {b} and {d}. In each column you see as many squares as the taller stack has.
Answer: {r}.

explain.all-cubes: {w_all_cubes} is all the cubes of the building. From the front the low stacks are covered by taller ones, so you see fewer.
explain.near-row: {w_near_row} is the near row only. But a far stack that is taller than the near one shows above it.
explain.far-row: {w_far_row} is the far row only. But if the near stack is taller, it covers the far one, and you see the near one.

G6.views.13.text: A building stands on a square of 3 × 3 cells. From the front you see stacks of height {a}, {b} and {c}, and from the side {d}, {e} and {f}. What is the greatest number of cubes the building can have?
solution: In each cell the stack can be no taller than both views allow, so we take the smaller of the two heights. In the first row the side height is {d}: {=min(a,d)} + {=min(b,d)} + {=min(c,d)} = {=min(a,d)+min(b,d)+min(c,d)}.
In the second row the side height is {e}: {=min(a,e)} + {=min(b,e)} + {=min(c,e)} = {=min(a,e)+min(b,e)+min(c,e)}.
In the third row the side height is {f}: {=min(a,f)} + {=min(b,f)} + {=min(c,f)} = {=min(a,f)+min(b,f)+min(c,f)}.
In all: {=min(a,d)+min(b,d)+min(c,d)} + {=min(a,e)+min(b,e)+min(c,e)} + {=min(a,f)+min(b,f)+min(c,f)} = {r}.
hints: For each cell of the base look at both views: how many cubes does the front view allow and how many does the side view allow? You cannot put more than the smaller of the two numbers.
There are nine cells. From the front the heights are {a}, {b}, {c}, from the side {d}, {e}, {f}: in each cell take the smaller of the two heights and add up all nine.
Answer: {r}.

explain.front-times-three: {w_front_times_three} is what you get if the three rows are the same and repeat the front view. But the height of a row is limited by the side view too: in each cell we take the smaller of the two heights.
explain.views-added: {w_views_added} is all the squares of the two views together. The building has more cubes: each of the nine cells has its own stack.
explain.all-tallest: {w_all_tallest} is {=9} × {=max(a,b,c)}: all nine stacks as tall as the tallest one. But the views do not allow that: in each cell we take the smaller of the two heights, which gives {r}.

G6.blocks.11.text: On the plan of a building made of cubes with edge 1 cm the heights of the stacks are written: in the first row {a} and {b}, in the second row {c} and {d}. What is the surface area of the building in square centimetres, not counting the part that stands on the table?
solution: From above you see one square for each of the 4 stacks: 4 cm².
Each stack has two sides facing outwards: 2 × ({a} + {b} + {c} + {d}) = {=2*(a+b+c+d)} cm².
Between neighbouring stacks you see steps as high as the difference of their heights: {=max(a,b)-min(a,b)} + {=max(c,d)-min(c,d)} + {=max(a,c)-min(a,c)} + {=max(b,d)-min(b,d)} = {s} cm².
The whole surface: 4 + {=2*(a+b+c+d)} + {s} = {r} cm².
hints: The surface has three parts: the top, the outer walls and the steps between stacks of different heights.
The top gives 4 cm². Each of the stacks {a}, {b}, {c}, {d} has two outer walls. A step between neighbours is the difference of their heights; there are four pairs of neighbours.
Answer: {r}.

explain.no-inner-steps: {w_no_inner_steps} leaves out the steps between stacks of different heights. They are part of the surface too, {s} cm² together, so the total is {r}.
explain.with-the-bottom: {w_with_the_bottom} counts the bottom too, but it stands on the table: 4 cm² too many. The surface is {r}.
explain.hidden-walls-counted: {w_hidden_walls_counted} is 4 + 4 × {=a+b+c+d}: all four walls of every stack were counted. But where stacks stand side by side, the walls are covered. We count the outer walls and the steps: {r}.

G6.blocks.12.text: A staircase has {a|stack|stacks|stacks}: the first is 1 cube high, and each next one is {b|cube|cubes|cubes} higher than the one before. How many cubes does the staircase have in all?
solution: The height of the last stack: 1 + ({a} − 1) × {b} = {=1+(a-1)*b}.
The first and the last stacks together have 1 + {=1+(a-1)*b} = {=2+(a-1)*b}, and the second and the last but one have just as many, and so on.
If we add all the stacks twice, in order and in reverse order, we get {=2+(a-1)*b} × {a} = {=(2+(a-1)*b)*a}; once is half of that: {=(2+(a-1)*b)*a} : 2 = {r}.
So the staircase has {r|cube|cubes|cubes}.
hints: Find the height of the last stack: it grows by {b|cube|cubes|cubes} with every stack.
The first and the last stack together have as many as the second and the last but one. How many such pairs do you get if you add everything twice, and what is the sum of a pair?
Answer: {r}.

explain.last-times-count: {w_last_times_count} is the number of stacks times the height of the last one. But the others are lower, and on average they have fewer cubes.
explain.pairs-not-halved: {w_pairs_not_halved} is the sum of a pair times the number of stacks. That counts every stack twice, so the result must be halved.
explain.last-tower: {w_last_tower} is the height of the last stack only, but we need the cubes of the whole staircase.

G6.blocks.13.text: A cube {a} × {a} × {a} was built from cubes, and then all the cubes that have no face on the outside were taken away. How many cubes are left?
solution: The cubes with no face outside are the ones inside. Take one layer off each of the six sides and an inner cube with side {a} − 2 = {=a-2} is left.
What is left is the outside: {=a*a*a} − {=(a-2)*(a-2)*(a-2)} = {r}.
So {r|cube is|cubes are|cubes are} left.
hints: The cubes inside were taken away, the ones on the outside are left. First find how many cubes are inside.
The inner cube is 2 shorter on every side: {a} − 2. Take it away from the whole cube.
Answer: {r}.

explain.faces-times-six: {w_faces_times_six} is six faces of {a} × {a}, but the cubes on the edges and in the corners were counted two and three times.
explain.one-layer-removed: {w_one_layer_removed} is {a} × {a} × {a} − {=a-1} × {=a-1} × {=a-1}: the inner cube was taken to have side {=a-1}. The inner cube is two cubes shorter on every side: {=a-2}.
explain.inner-cube: {w_inner_cube} is the cubes inside, which are the ones taken away. What is left is the shell: {=a*a*a} − {w_inner_cube} = {r}.

G7.plan.11.text: You are facing north. First you turn right by {a|quarter turn|quarter turns|quarter turns}, and then left by {b|quarter turn|quarter turns|quarter turns}. Which way are you facing now? 1) north; 2) east; 3) south; 4) west. Answer with the number of the option.
solution: A turn to the right goes round the circle north, east, south, west, and a turn to the left goes the other way.
Left cancels the same amount of right, so we take the difference: {a} − {b} = {=a-b}.
A whole turn is 4 quarters and changes nothing, so what is left is {=mod(a-b+8,4)|step|steps|steps} round the circle to the right of north: that is option {r}.
hints: A turn to the left cancels a turn to the right. First think how many quarters you have turned to the right in the end.
Find the difference {a} − {b}: if it is negative, you ended up turned to the left. Drop whole turns of 4 quarters.
Answer: {r}.

solution: Going clockwise, north is 0 degrees, east is 90, south is 180 and west is 270.
A full turn is 360 degrees and changes nothing. Left over: {=mod(a,360)} degrees.
An angle of {=mod(a,360)} degrees lies between {=mod(a,360)-45} and {=mod(a,360)+45} degrees, exactly halfway between two main directions.

G7.plan-1S.12.text: On one map 1 cm stands for {p} km, and on another map for {a} km. On the first map two cities are {c} cm apart. How many centimetres apart are these cities on the second map?

G7.plan-1S.13.text: On a map 1 cm stands for {a} km. The cities are {b} cm apart on the map. Two cyclists set off at the same time from these cities towards each other, at {c} km/h and {d} km/h. After how many hours do they meet?
